source: Modelled on NASA and commercial Earth-observation small satellites (NASA Earth Science Technology Office CubeSat missions, Landsat and Sentinel-2 for imaging requirements, Planet's Dove constellation for the small end). Sun-synchronous orbit geometry, eclipse and ground-contact fractions are computed from first principles; atmospheric density follows the piecewise-exponential table in the body catalog (mean solar activity). The five-year disposal rule is the 2022 FCC orbital debris rule that NASA missions also follow. Budget and part costs are representative of university and small-company missions.
units: orbit.options: altitude_km of a circular sun-synchronous orbit and beta_angle_deg, the angle between the orbit plane and the Sun (22 degrees for a mid-morning orbit, about 75 for a dawn-dusk orbit that almost never enters shadow). orbit.station_*: latitude and number of ground stations and the lowest elevation at which a pass counts. drag_coefficient and body_frontal_area_m2 set the drag (half the solar array area is added). reentry_altitude_km: where the satellite burns up. deorbit_perigee_km: the perigee a disposal burn must reach. debris_rule_years: how soon after the mission the satellite must be gone. required_gsd_m: the coarsest ground resolution that still serves the imaging objective. Fields about landing (sites, descent, landing_window, route, entry, sky) are unused here and kept at neutral values. objectives: area_imaged_mkm2 is millions of square kilometres imaged at the required resolution or better; days_operated counts days until the mission ended. orbit.options.image_quality (0-1) scales the ground that counts as usefully imaged: low Sun and long shadows spoil pictures of fields. art: path of the mission card picture relative to the site root (a render of the destination by the game engine from the maps in surface_maps.json).
name: Earth observation small satellite
tagline: Watch the world’s farmland from orbit, on a university budget.
briefing: A food-security agency wants fresh pictures of the world’s croplands every few days, sharp enough to tell one field from the next, for a year. You have the budget of a small satellite, not a flagship. Choose a frame, a camera and a radio, find a cheap ride to orbit, and decide how high to fly: low orbits see more detail and fall out of the sky sooner; high orbits last for decades, which is a problem of its own. This is the place to learn how mass, power, data and money pull against each other.

options.name: Low orbit, 420 km
options.summary: As low as the Space Station. The sharpest pictures and an orbit that cleans itself up; without a thruster the air drags the satellite down within the year.

options.name: Rideshare orbit, 525 km
options.summary: Where the cheap shared launches go. A sound compromise: good detail, a few years of natural life, home within the disposal rule.

options.name: Mid orbit, 650 km
options.summary: A wider view and longer passes over the ground station. Details blur, and a dead satellite would stay up for decades: it needs a way down.

options.name: Dawn-dusk orbit, 525 km
options.summary: Rides the line between day and night, in sunlight nearly all the time: power is never a problem. The ground below is always at sunrise or sunset, with long shadows across every field.

descent.summary: From a 100 km orbit to a soft touchdown.

objectives.name: Image the croplands, field by field
objectives.summary: Cover as much ground as you can at 10 m detail or better. All the world’s cropland is about 16 million km²: revisit it again and again through the seasons.

objectives.name: Get the pictures to the ground
objectives.summary: An image in the recorder helps nobody. The radio and the passes decide what the agency actually receives.

objectives.name: Work through a full growing year
objectives.summary: Crops are judged by how they change. A satellite that stops in spring misses the harvest.

objectives.name: Carry a second experiment
objectives.summary: A spare corner of the satellite can host another measurement: ships, weather or ground temperature.

reference_design.name: Rideshare microsatellite
reference_design.summary: A microsatellite with fold-out wings, a compact imager, reaction wheels and an S-band radio, on a shared launch to 525 km.

nasa_reference.mission: Landsat and NASA’s small-satellite Earth science missions
nasa_reference.summary: NASA has imaged every field on Earth since 1972 with Landsat: a sun-synchronous orbit at 705 km, crossing the equator mid-morning so the light is the same on every pass. Small satellites now fill the gaps between its 16-day revisits. They fly lower and cheaper, ride to orbit with dozens of others, and live or die by the same budgets: enough power through every eclipse, enough passes to empty the recorder, and a way out of orbit when the work is done.
